newsitem.title: USA: No unusual Iraq moves in south -- U.S. officer.
newsitem.headline: No unusual Iraq moves in south -- U.S. officer.

text.p: A U.S. naval officer said on Tuesday that American warplanes monitoring southern Iraq have seen no unusual Iraqi military movements in the area in recent months despite opposition reports of government offensives there.
"We have seen nothing unusual or out of the ordinary," Captain Larry Baucom, commanding officer of the aircraft carrier Carl Vinson, told reporters.
"It has been about the same since we have been here," he said, adding the Carl Vinson battlegroup has been in the Gulf for over two months.

Baucom was responding to reporters who asked whether U.S. warplanes had noticed unusual Iraqi military movements in the south. Iraqi opposition groups have reported a series of government attacks on opposition supporters in the south over the period.

U.S. Navy pilot Lieutnant Mike Smith, 27, from Galion, Ohio, who flies South Watch sorties from the Carl Vinson, told reporters: "There hasn't been much going on (in the south). It has been all in the north."
U.S., British and French pilots fly regular sorties over southern Iraq in a programme called Southern Watch started in 1992 to prevent Iraqi planes from flying south of the 32nd parallel.

The United States and Western Gulf War allies Britain and France set up the no-fly zone in southern Iraq to help protect Shi'ites who were crushed by government forces when they tried to rebel against President Saddam Hussein after the 1991 Gulf War.

Mohammad Baqer Hakim, chairman of the Iran-based Iraqi opposition Supreme Council for the Islamic Revolution in Iraq, said on Monday the Iraqi government had started what he called several offensives in the south over the past two months, the latest of which began on August 27.
He told the Kuwait News Agency a big offensive was expected this week as Iraqi army tanks and artillery units and Republican Guard troops had been taking up new positoions in the south.
